Photograph: BBC Queensland Child safety officer incorrectly assessed Elizabeth Struhs as ‘safe’ day after she was admitted to hospital in coma Inquest into death of eight-year-old Queensland girl who was denied insulin by her religious parents told her case was complex Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Andrew Messenger Wed 14 Oct 2026 04.08 EDT Last modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 05.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A child safety officer incorrectly assessed Elizabeth Struhs as “safe” one day after she arrived at hospital in a coma and nearly died due to the neglect of her parents, a coroner’s court has heard. A Queensland coronial inquest heard evidence on Wednesday from one of the two child safety officers who ultimately decided to return the then six-year-old, who had type 1 diabetes, to the care of her parents at their home in Toowoomba. She died there on 7 January 2022 while her parents, Kerrie and Jason, and other members of their small religious sect prayed for her miraculous healing or resurrection. None of the witnesses can be identified for legal reasons. The child safety officer was given the duty of investigating Elizabeth’s home after she presented to Toowoomba hospital in a coma suffering from diabetic ketoacidosis on 17 July 2019. He later became her case worker. Just one day later – after she was transferred to the Queensland children’s hospital in Brisbane – another child safety officer who assisted him completed an initial safety assessment of Elizabeth. She marked her “safe”. But her colleague told the court on Wednesday that Elizabeth should have been recorded as “unsafe” because they didn’t have enough information about her circumstances at the time. 5:49 Fourteen members of religious sect found guilty of killing eight-year-old Elizabeth Struhs - video Elizabeth was later assessed as a child in need of protection, a legal standard under the child safety act. In 2021, both Jason and Kerrie were convicted of not providing the necessaries of life to their daughter as a result of the 2019 incident, and Kerrie was jailed. The child safety officer later had a conversation with a doctor from the Queensland children’s hospital who told him Elizabeth was lucky not to have died and that Kerrie had not shown remorse as a result of the incident. The doctor said Kerrie continued to not believe in medicine and that it would be unsafe for her daughter to live with her until she changed her views, the inquest heard. “The pressure on dad around such strong religious beliefs will be difficult,” the doctor told him, according to his contemporaneous notes presented in court on Wednesday. “The team feel that the only way to force mum to see the concerns may be for Elizabeth to be out of home.” Elizabeth was sent home despite the objections of the Brisbane-based specialist paediatric doctors. The doctor told the court on Monday that she felt “stonewalled” by the officer after raising concerns about Elizabeth’s safety at home. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Elizabeth was ultimately returned home to live with her family, with an intervention parental agreement: a short-term, voluntary arrangement that allows child safety authorities to aid a child in danger without a child protection order, the inquest heard. On Wednesday, the child safety officer said that the safety plan they adopted for Elizabeth “in hindsight, could have been more robust”. But he said he didn’t have a clear recollection of a meeting in which they discussed the idea of adopting the plan. “I do recall being in two minds about the best outcome for Elizabeth and her siblings, specifically Elizabeth being able to remain at home and connected with her family or out of home,” he said in a written statement provided to the court. He said it was a difficult decision and that there were practical considerations of how to manage the complex case. The child safety officer said it was significant that Jason had repeatedly committed to provide insulin for his daughter. Elizabeth required daily insulin injections to live. The inquest previously heard Jason, a longtime sceptic of his wife’s religion, subsequently provided medical attention for Elizabeth for two years. But he ceased doing so after being convinced to convert and then to stop treating her by the members of the group, and he stopped her insulin in late 2021, causing her death. All 14 adult members of the sect – known as the Saints – were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including the group leader, Brendan Stevens. The inquest continues. https://www.koreaherald.com/article/1089.text: Parliamentary speaker Cho discusses energy, defense cooperation with Croatian president Published : Oct. 10, 2026 - 12:39:25 Add The Korea Herald on Google Bookmark Event Link copied! National Assembly Speaker Cho Jeong-sik (left) poses for a photo with Croatian President Zoran Milanovic in Zagreb, Croatia, Saturday, in this photo provided by his office. National Assembly Speaker Cho Jeong-sik has held a series of meetings with Croatian President Zoran Milanovic, Parliament Speaker Gordan Jandrokovic and Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic to seek energy and defense cooperation between the two nations, his office said Saturday. In a meeting with the Croatian president in Zagreb on Friday (local time), Cho said the two countries have been maintaining friendly, cooperative relations since establishing diplomatic ties in 1992, which were upgraded to a comprehensive, future-oriented partnership in 2023. Cho has been on a four-nation trip to Italy, Vatican City, Croatia and Greece over nine days. National Assembly Speaker Cho Jeong-sik (left) poses for a photo with Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic in Zagreb, Croatia, Saturday, in this photo provided by his office. In a separate meeting with the Croatian prime minister, Cho also said the two countries should solidify their ties in the economy, culture, defense and energy sectors, highlighting a recent arms supply deal. Last month, South Korean defense firm Hanwha Aerospace signed a deal to export 18 Chunmoo multiple launch rocket systems (MLRS) to Croatia in an arms contract worth some 640 billion won (US$477 million), marking the first major arms deal between the two countries, opening up avenues for greater partnership beyond arms exports, such as industrial cooperation and military logistics support. Croatia has become the fourth European country to acquire the Chunmoo system, following Poland, Estonia and Norway.
